reference.source: Brukner and Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine
clinicalPearls: Presents with lateral shoulder pain aggravated by overhead activity and by lying on the affected side at night
Chronic cuff 'tendinitis' is predominantly a degenerative tendinopathy (tendinosis) reflecting failed healing under repetitive load, rather than a primarily inflammatory process
A painful arc through mid-range abduction is characteristic, with Hawkins-Kennedy and Neer signs supporting subacromial involvement
Resisted testing helps localise the affected tendon (empty-can/Jobe for supraspinatus, resisted external rotation for infraspinatus and teres minor)
Ultrasound and MRI distinguish tendinopathy from partial- or full-thickness tears and assess the subacromial space
Management is largely conservative with relative rest, activity and load modification, and progressive or eccentric loading with scapular rehabilitation guided by physiotherapy
A subacromial corticosteroid injection may give short-term relief, but repeated injections risk tendon weakening and should be used judiciously
The concept of 'impingement' is increasingly reframed as rotator cuff related shoulder pain, emphasising intrinsic tendon change over purely mechanical compression
reference.pathophysiology: The rotator cuff tendons, especially supraspinatus, are exposed to repetitive tensile and compressive load, particularly during overhead activity. When chronic overload outstrips the tendon's capacity to repair, a degenerative tendinopathy develops, characterised by disorganised collagen, increased ground substance, neovascularisation and relatively little classic inflammation, which is why the term tendinosis is preferred to tendinitis. Narrowing of the subacromial space from acromial shape, bursal thickening, or dynamic scapular and cuff dysfunction can add mechanical irritation. Over time the weakened tendon may progress to partial- or full-thickness tearing.
additionalDifferentials: Rotator cuff tear (partial or full thickness)
Cervical radiculopathy referring to the shoulder
Glenohumeral instability with secondary cuff pain
additionalInvestigations: Ultrasound to assess tendon integrity, thickness and bursal change, including dynamic assessment
MRI to characterise tendinopathy, tears and cuff muscle atrophy
Plain radiographs to assess acromial morphology, calcification and arthritis
Diagnostic subacromial local anaesthetic injection to confirm the pain source
Clinical provocative testing (painful arc, Hawkins-Kennedy, Neer, resisted cuff tests)
redFlags: Sudden loss of active elevation after trauma suggesting an acute large cuff tear
Systemic features such as fever, weight loss or night sweats raising infection or malignancy
Fixed global restriction of passive movement suggesting frozen shoulder or joint pathology
Neurological deficit pointing to cervical spine or nerve involvement
reference.prognosis: Most cases improve with structured loading rehabilitation over weeks to months, although recovery can be slow and recurrence is common if load is not managed; large or full-thickness tears may need surgical consideration.
pitfalls: Labelling all cuff pain as inflammatory and relying on rest rather than progressive loading
Repeated corticosteroid injections that may weaken the tendon and mask progression to tearing
Overlooking scapular dyskinesis and the wider kinetic chain in rehabilitation
Missing a full-thickness tear that requires different management
references: Brukner and Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine
management: Progressive and eccentric loading with scapular rehabilitation, guided by physiotherapy, as the mainstay of treatment
Relative rest with activity and load modification, avoiding aggravating overhead positions
Simple analgesia or NSAIDs for symptom control
Judicious subacromial corticosteroid injection for persistent pain limiting engagement with rehabilitation
Addressing biomechanical contributors such as posture, scapular dyskinesis and overhead technique
Surgical referral for subacromial decompression or repair reserved for refractory cases or an associated significant tear
